questions.why: You must now meet the contract. On a put, that means you buy the shares at the strike. Here's how it reached you. A holder exercised. OCC assigned that exercise at random to a broker that clears options. That broker passed it to a customer short that series, and that's you.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise is the holder's move. Assignment is what lands on the writer.

wrong.You just used your right to act: That's exercise, and only a holder exercises. Assignment is the other side of it.
wrong.You bought back the put early: That's a closing purchase. Do that first and you can't be assigned.
wrong.Your options approval came in: Brokers do approve you for options. That has nothing to do with assignment.

questions.simple: You must now meet the contract, because a holder exercised and the notice landed on you.

questions.q: Your call is deep in the money. You tell your broker to use it and buy the shares at the strike. What's that called?
questions.why: Exercise. You're using the right the call gives you, so you buy the stock at the strike. A put holder who exercises sells at the strike. The writer on the other side gets the assignment. Know one thing before you do it. Exercise early and you throw away any time value left. Selling the call keeps it.
questions.lesson_line: Exercising early throws away the time value. Selling the option keeps it.

wrong.Assignment: Assignment lands on the writer after a holder exercises. You're the holder.
wrong.Expiration: Expiration is the date the option ends. Using the right is exercise.
wrong.Rolling: Rolling closes one option and opens another. Nothing gets bought at the strike.

questions.simple: Exercise, because you're using the call's right to buy the shares at the strike.

deeper.example: In OIC's example, exercising instead of selling throws away $0.80 of time value. Sell the option in the market and that time value stays in the price you get.

questions.q: You own a call on a US stock, and the chain lists it as American-style. What does that tell you?
choices: It's listed on a US exchange
It settles in cash, not shares
questions.why: Any day until it expires. That's all American-style means. Every standard US stock option works this way, so it's what you'll see on the stocks we trade. European-style is the other kind, exercised only around expiration, and most index options are European. The style is about when you can exercise. It says nothing about where it trades or how it settles.
questions.lesson_line: The style tells you when you can exercise. Not where it trades.

wrong.Exercise only at expiry: That's European-style, the other exercise style.
wrong.It's listed on a US exchange: The style is about when you can exercise, not where it trades. Most index options are European-style.
wrong.It settles in cash, not shares: That's settlement, a separate term. An exercised stock call delivers shares, while index options mostly settle in cash.

questions.simple: You can exercise it any day until it expires, because that's what American style means.

questions.q: The chain shows implied volatility of 80% on one stock and 30% on another. What is the 80% telling you?
choices: It moved more in the past
The odds the option pays off
questions.why: The market expects a bigger move in that stock. Implied volatility is read from the option's price. It's the size of move the market is pricing in, either way. That's different from how much the stock already moved, which is historical volatility. At 80% you pay more for the options, because you're buying a bigger expected move.
questions.lesson_line: Implied volatility is the move the market expects. Historical volatility is the move that already happened.

wrong.It moved more in the past: That's historical volatility, what already happened.
wrong.The odds the option pays off: Some traders read delta that way. Implied volatility is about the size of the move.
wrong.How fast time value decays: That's theta, the daily cost of time.

questions.simple: The market expects a bigger move in that stock, and you pay more for its options.

questions.q: You think a stock is headed lower. You buy a put on it and own no shares. What's this position called?
questions.why: A long put. You bought the put on its own to profit if the stock drops. The most you can lose is the premium you paid. Shorting the stock is a different animal, because there the risk has no ceiling. A protective put is one you buy against shares you already own. A naked put is sold, not bought.
questions.lesson_line: A long put caps your risk at the premium. Shorting the stock doesn't.

wrong.Protective put: A protective put hedges shares you own. You don't own any.
wrong.Naked put: A naked put is sold, not bought. It profits if the stock holds up.
wrong.Covered call: A covered call is a call you sell against owned shares. It's not a bet on a drop.

questions.simple: A long put, a put you buy by itself to profit from a drop, and you can only lose what you paid.

questions.q: A stock's implied volatility jumps ahead of its earnings report. That tells you the market expects the stock to go up.
questions.why: False. Implied volatility is the size of the move the market expects, not the direction. Puts get pricier right along with calls. So high implied volatility means expensive options, not a bullish market. Buy calls into that report and you're paying up for a big move either way.
questions.lesson_line: High implied volatility means expensive options. It says nothing about direction.
questions.simple: False, because implied volatility shows how big a move is expected, not which way it goes.

deeper.counter: A call buyer and a put buyer on the same stock both pay for high implied volatility. That is the point: the premium prices a big move in either direction. High implied volatility before a report says the market expects a large move, not a rally.

questions.story: You bought the 50-strike put to hedge. The stock just slid to $47.
questions.q: Where does your put stand right now?
questions.why: In the money. A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike, and $47 is under $50. That's your hedge doing its job: the put gains as the stock slides. Puts flip the call rule. In the money doesn't mean anything's been used, though. You choose what happens next. Hold the put, sell it or exercise it.
questions.lesson_line: Puts flip the rule. Below the strike is in the money.

wrong.Out of the money: That would be a 50-strike call with the stock at $47. Your put is the opposite.
wrong.At the money: At the money needs the stock sitting right on the $50 strike.
wrong.Exercised: Exercise is something you choose to do. Being in the money doesn't do it for you.

questions.simple: In the money, because the stock at $47 is below your $50 put strike.

deeper.example: Same stock at $47, two contracts. The 50-strike put is in the money, since a put needs the stock under its strike. The 50-strike call is out of the money, since a call needs it above. Same strike, same price, opposite answers.

questions.q: A cheap call catches your eye: the 100 strike for $1.20, with the stock at $95. How much intrinsic value are you buying?
questions.why: $0. For a call, intrinsic value is the stock minus the strike, and it can't go below zero. $95 minus $100 is under zero, so it's $0. Every cent of that $1.20 is time value. You're paying for the chance the stock gets above 100 before the date. That's fine, as long as you know it going in.
questions.lesson_line: Out of the money, you're paying for time and a move. Nothing more.
questions.simple: $0, because the stock at $95 is below the 100 strike, so all of the $1.20 is time value.

wrong.$1.20: That's the whole premium. Out of the money, all of it is time value.
wrong.-$5: Intrinsic value stops at zero. It never goes negative.
wrong.$5: That's put math, strike minus stock. You're holding a call.

questions.q: The stock is at $64. The 60-strike call costs $5.10. How much of that price are you paying for time?
questions.why: $1.10. Start with intrinsic value, the in-the-money part. $64 minus $60 is $4.00. Everything above that is time value. $5.10 minus $4.00 is $1.10. So $4.00 of the price is real today, and $1.10 is time that melts to zero by expiration.
questions.lesson_line: Split every premium: what's real today, and what's time.
questions.simple: $1.10, because $4.00 of the $5.10 is the in-the-money part and the rest is time.

wrong.$4.00: That's the intrinsic value, the in-the-money part. Time value is what's left over.
wrong.$5.10: That's the whole premium. Take the intrinsic value out first.
wrong.$9.10: You added the intrinsic value instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: You buy the 60-strike call for $2.50 and plan to hold it to expiration. Where does the stock need to be just to break even?
questions.why: $62.50. You paid $2.50 a share, so the stock has to earn that back before you make a dime. $60 plus $2.50 is $62.50 at expiration, before fees. Between $60 and $62.50 the call is in the money and you're still losing. So when you pick a strike, look at the breakeven, not just the strike.
questions.lesson_line: Your line is strike plus premium, not the strike.
questions.simple: $62.50, because the stock has to cover the $2.50 you paid on top of the 60 strike.

wrong.$60.00: That's the strike. You forgot the $2.50 you paid.
wrong.$57.50: You subtracted the premium. That's put math.
wrong.$2.50: That's the premium, not a stock price.

questions.q: Your call has a delta of 0.40. The stock pops $2 and nothing else changes. About how much does the option gain per share?
questions.why: About $0.80. Delta is roughly how much the option moves for each $1 in the stock. 0.40 times 2 is 0.80 a share. It's a rough guide, not a promise. Delta keeps changing as the stock moves, so the real number will be a bit off. Use it to know about what a move is worth to you.
questions.lesson_line: Delta gets you close, not exact.
questions.simple: About $0.80, because a 0.40 delta moves the option about $0.40 for each $1, and the stock moved $2.

deeper.counter: Delta keeps changing during market hours, so the $0.80 is an estimate, not a promise. It will typically not predict the exact change in the premium.

wrong.$0.40: That's one dollar's worth. The stock moved $2.
wrong.$2.00: That's the stock's move, as if delta were 1.
wrong.$5.00: You divided the move by delta. Multiply instead.

questions.q: Your option shows a theta of -0.06. If the stock sits still all day, about what does one contract lose?
questions.why: About $6. Theta is per share, per day. One standard contract is 100 shares, so 0.06 times 100 is 6. The minus sign just means it's a loss. Six bucks a day doesn't sound like much. Over a few flat weeks it adds up, and decay tends to pick up speed near expiration.
questions.lesson_line: Theta is per share. Times 100 is what a quiet day costs you.
questions.simple: About $6, because a theta of 0.06 is per share per day, and one contract is 100 shares.

wrong.$0.06: That's per share. You skipped the 100 shares.
wrong.$0.60: That's ten shares, not a hundred.

questions.story: You bought 5 calls into a breakout last week. The stock ran and the calls are up nicely. You want to take the win.
questions.q: Which order gets you out?
questions.why: Sell to close. You bought the calls, so you're long them, and a closing sale ends a long position. Sell to open would write 5 new calls, the opposite of what you want. Buy to close is for a short option. Exercise would buy the shares and throw away the time value left. Read the ticket twice before you hit send.
questions.lesson_line: Buy to open, sell to close. Sell to open, buy to close.

wrong.Sell to open: That writes new calls and opens a short. It doesn't close the ones you own.
wrong.Buy to close: That closes a short option. You're long these calls.
wrong.Exercise them: That buys the shares at the strike and throws away the time value left.

questions.simple: Sell to close, because you own the calls and a closing sale ends a long position.

questions.q: You own 100 shares and write a covered call against them. That call adds to your downside if the stock drops.
questions.why: False. The short call doesn't add downside risk. If the stock drops, you lose on the shares exactly as you would without the call. You keep the premium either way, so it softens the hit a little. What the call costs you is the upside past the strike.
questions.lesson_line: A covered call doesn't add downside. It sells off your upside.
questions.simple: False, because the call you sold adds no downside, and the shares carry the same risk as before.

questions.story: A stock you like trades at $52. You'd love to own it at $50. You sell the 50-strike put and keep enough cash set aside to buy 100 shares.
questions.q: What's this strategy called?
questions.why: A cash-secured put. You write the put and park the cash to buy the shares if you're assigned. The 50 strike is below the $52 price, so the goal is to get assigned and own it at 50. A naked put is the same sale with no cash set aside. Only pick a strike you'd honestly be glad to pay.
questions.lesson_line: Only sell a put at a price you'd be glad to pay for the shares.

wrong.Protective put: A protective put is bought to hedge shares you own. You sold a put.
wrong.Naked put: A naked put has no cash set aside to buy the shares. Yours does.
wrong.Put credit spread: That spread also buys a lower put. You sold one put and bought none.

questions.simple: A cash-secured put, because you sold the put and kept the cash ready to buy the shares.

deeper.trap: Don't pick the strike for the premium alone. OIC says you have to be comfortable with the strike as a long-term buying price, no matter how low the market goes. If the stock falls far below $50, you still buy at $50.

questions.q: You're up big in a stock and want a floor under it. You buy a put against your shares. What's that called?
questions.why: A protective put. You add a long put to shares you already own. The strike becomes your floor. However far the stock drops, you can sell at the strike until the put expires. It works like insurance: you pay the premium and hope you never need it. Buy the put at the same time as the stock and it's called a married put.
questions.lesson_line: A protective put is insurance. You pay for it and hope you never use it.

wrong.A cash-secured put: That's a put you sell with cash set aside to buy. It adds shares, not protection.
wrong.A covered call: That's a call you sell against your shares. It puts no floor under them.
wrong.A naked put: A naked put is sold, not bought. It's a duty to buy, the opposite of protection.

questions.simple: A protective put, because you bought a put on shares you own to set a floor under them.

questions.story: You own 100 shares from $80. They're at $98 now. You buy the 95-strike put and sell the 105-strike call, same expiry.
questions.q: What did you just build?
questions.why: A collar. You sold a call and bought a put, same date, against shares you already own. The 95 put is your floor. The 105 call is your ceiling. The premium from the call helps pay for the put. So until expiry, your exit sits somewhere between 95 and 105.
questions.lesson_line: A collar buys a floor by selling your ceiling.

wrong.Covered call: A covered call has no put, so no floor under the shares.
wrong.Long strangle: A long strangle buys a call and a put. You sold the call.
wrong.Bull call spread: That's two calls, one bought and one sold. You hold shares and a put.

questions.simple: A collar, because you own the stock, bought a put below and sold a call above, same date.

questions.q: You buy the 50 call and sell the 55 call on the same stock, same expiry. What kind of spread is that?
questions.why: A vertical spread. Same type, same date, two strikes. Buy the 50 call and sell the 55 and you've built a bull call spread, one kind of vertical. You pay a net debit to open it, and that debit is the most you can lose. A calendar or a diagonal uses two dates. A straddle pairs a call with a put.
questions.lesson_line: A vertical: same type, same date, two strikes.

wrong.Calendar spread: A calendar uses two dates. Yours share one.
wrong.Diagonal spread: A diagonal uses two dates and two strikes. Yours share a date.
wrong.Straddle: A straddle pairs a call with a put. You used two calls.

questions.simple: A vertical spread, because both calls share a date and differ only in strike.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.story: You log a trade in your Journal and it labels the row Put Credit Spread. The legs: sell the 45 put, buy the 40 put, same expiry.
questions.q: What's the textbook name for it?
questions.why: A bull put spread. Same trade, two names. You sell the higher put and buy the lower one, and you collect a credit to open. It does well if the stock holds or rises. A bear put spread is the reverse: buy the higher put, sell the lower, pay a debit. So when the Journal says Put Credit Spread, read bull put spread.
questions.lesson_line: Put credit spread, bull put spread. Same trade.

wrong.Bear put spread: That buys the higher put and sells the lower one, for a debit. It's the bearish version.
wrong.Protective put: That's a put bought against shares you own. There are no shares here.
wrong.Long strangle: That buys a call and a put. You sold one put and bought another.

questions.simple: A bull put spread, because you sold the higher put and bought the lower one for a credit.

reasons: rests on the Journal's label (prettyStrategyType), which can change

questions.q: You open a bull call spread and your cash balance drops by the net amount you paid. What kind of spread is it?
questions.why: A debit spread. It costs you money to open, so your cash goes down. A bull call spread is one, and so is a bear put spread. On a bull call spread, the debit you pay is the most you can lose. A credit spread is the flip side: you get paid to open it. Calendars and diagonals are about dates, not cash.
questions.lesson_line: Debit, you pay to open. Credit, you get paid.

wrong.Credit spread: A credit spread pays you to open it. Your cash went down.
wrong.Calendar spread: A calendar uses two dates. Debit or credit is about cash.
wrong.Diagonal spread: A diagonal changes the date and the strike. That says nothing about cash.

questions.simple: A debit spread, because it cost you money to open and your cash went down.

questions.q: A stock reports tonight. You expect a big move but can't call the direction. You buy a call and a put, same strike and date. What's that?
questions.why: A long straddle. One strike, one date, a call and a put, both bought. It pays if the stock moves big either way. The catch is you pay two premiums, so the bar to break even is high. And implied volatility can get bid up before a report, so both legs can cost you more. You need a big move just to get paid.
questions.lesson_line: A straddle bets on size, not direction. You pay two premiums for it.

wrong.A long strangle: A strangle uses two strikes. You used one.
wrong.A short straddle: Writing both is a short straddle. You bought both.
wrong.A married put: That's buying the stock with a put. There's no stock here.

questions.simple: A long straddle, because you bought a call and a put at one strike to profit from a big move either way.

questions.story: The stock is at $100. You buy the 110-strike call and the 90-strike put, same expiry.
questions.q: What did you just put on?
questions.why: A long strangle. You bought a call above the stock and a put below it, both out of the money, same date. From $100, the stock has to get past $110 or under $90 before either leg is worth anything at expiration. Then it still has to cover both premiums. That's why a strangle costs less than a straddle but needs a bigger move. A straddle would use one strike for both.
questions.lesson_line: A strangle is cheaper than a straddle. It needs a bigger move to pay.

wrong.Long straddle: A straddle uses one strike for both. Yours are at $110 and $90.
wrong.Iron condor: An iron condor sells a call and a put and buys further-out ones. You only bought.
wrong.Collar: A collar needs shares you own, plus a call you sold.

questions.simple: A long strangle, because you bought a call above $100 and a put below it, two strikes, same date.

questions.q: You sell this Friday's 50 call and buy the 50 call two months out, same stock. What's that spread called?
questions.why: A calendar spread. Same strike, same type, two dates. You sell the near one and buy the later one. The idea is time. Decay tends to speed up close to expiration, so the call you sold melts faster than the one you own. You'll also hear it called a time spread or a horizontal spread. A diagonal changes the strike too, a vertical keeps one date, and a butterfly uses three strikes.
questions.lesson_line: A calendar: one strike, two dates.

wrong.Diagonal spread: A diagonal changes the strike too. Yours share the 50.
wrong.Vertical spread: A vertical keeps one date and uses two strikes.

questions.simple: A calendar spread, because you sold the near call and bought the later one at the same strike.

questions.q: You buy the 50 call two months out and sell the 55 call that expires this week. That's a diagonal spread.
questions.why: True. Two calls, different strikes and different dates. That's a diagonal. Change only the date and you've got a calendar. Change only the strike and you've got a vertical. You changed both.
questions.lesson_line: A diagonal is a calendar and a vertical in one.
questions.simple: True, because a diagonal changes both the strike and the date.

questions.q: You sell a call and buy a higher one, and sell a put and buy a lower one, all on one date. Which two spreads is that?
choices: Bear call spread plus bull put spread
Bull call spread plus bull put spread
questions.answer: Bear call spread plus bull put spread
questions.why: A bear call spread plus a bull put spread. Put together, that's an iron condor sold for a credit. You want the stock to stay in a range. If it finishes between the two short strikes, everything expires worthless and you keep the credit. The most you can lose is one side's width, less that credit.
questions.lesson_line: An iron condor is two credit spreads around the price. It wants a quiet stock.

wrong.Bull call spread plus bull put spread: A bull call spread buys the lower call. You sold the lower call and bought the higher one.
wrong.Long straddle plus long strangle: Those both buy options. Here you sold the inside call and put.
wrong.Covered call plus protective put: That's a collar on shares you own. There are no shares here.

questions.simple: A bear call spread plus a bull put spread, and together they make an iron condor.

questions.q: Your Journal shows an iron condor and an iron butterfly side by side. Looking at the legs, what sets the butterfly apart?
choices: It sells a call and put at one strike
It is built only from calls, no puts
It costs a net debit when you open it
Its loss has no limit if the stock runs
questions.answer: It sells a call and put at one strike
questions.why: Look at the short legs. The butterfly sells its call and its put at the same strike, the body. Then it buys a call above and a put below, the wings. A condor splits that body into two strikes. So the butterfly wants the stock to finish near one price, while the condor gives you a range. Both take in cash up front. The most a butterfly can lose is body to wing, less the credit.
questions.lesson_line: Butterfly: one body strike. Condor: two.

wrong.It is built only from calls, no puts: That's a long call butterfly. The iron version uses calls and puts.
wrong.It costs a net debit when you open it: Debit or credit doesn't separate them. Sold the usual way, both take in cash up front.
wrong.Its loss has no limit if the stock runs: The call bought above the body caps that loss. The most it can lose is body to wing, less the credit.

questions.simple: The butterfly sells its call and put at one strike, while the condor sells them at two.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass; key reworded again here

questions.q: Buy one 50 call, sell two 55 calls and buy one 60 call, all one date. That's a long call butterfly.
questions.why: True. One, two, one. You buy the low call, sell two in the middle and buy the high one. It does best with the stock right at 55, the body, at expiration. The most you can lose is what you paid to open it. You're betting on where the stock lands.
questions.lesson_line: A butterfly bets on a price. The most you can lose is what you paid.
questions.simple: True, because a long call butterfly buys one low call, sells two middle calls and buys one high call.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Calls and puts with over nine months to expiration when listed are called ___.
questions.why: LEAPS. That's the name for long-dated calls and puts with an expiration over nine months away when listed. More time to expiration means more time value, all else equal. So a LEAPS contract tends to carry more time value than a shorter-dated one.
questions.lesson_line: LEAPS buy time, and time costs more premium.
questions.simple: LEAPS are long-dated calls and puts with more than nine months to go when they are first listed.

reasons: a number in a definition (over nine months when listed)

questions.q: Your call expires Friday and the setup still looks good. In one order you close it and open the same strike a month out. What's that?
questions.why: That's a roll. You close the open option and open a new one at a different date, a different strike or both. Both trades go in at the same time. Exercise uses your right to buy the shares, so nothing new opens. Averaging down is buying more of the same option cheaper. Just know a roll isn't free, because you're paying for fresh time.
questions.lesson_line: A roll is two trades at once: a close and a new open.

wrong.Exercising it early: Exercise buys the shares at the strike. It opens no new option, so it's not a roll.
wrong.Averaging down: That's buying more of the same option at a lower price to cut your cost.
wrong.Letting it expire: Letting it expire ends the option. A roll closes it and opens the next one at once.

questions.simple: Rolling, because you closed one option and opened another at a new date in one move.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My iron condor has four options. Each one is a ___ of the trade.
questions.why: Leg. A leg is one side of a position with two or more sides. This iron condor has four: a short call, a long call above it, a short put and a long put below it. Opening one leg first and hoping for a better price on the rest is legging in. OIC calls that the higher-risk way.
questions.lesson_line: Legging in one side at a time is the riskier way to open a spread.
questions.simple: Each option in a spread is one leg, so this iron condor has four legs.

questions.q: Before you buy a call, you pull up a table of every contract on the stock, sorted by expiry and strike. What's that table?
questions.why: The option chain. It lists every contract on one stock, set out by expiration date and strike. For each one you'll see the bid, the ask, volume, open interest, implied volatility and the Greeks. Check the bid and the ask first. A wide gap between them costs you on the way in and again on the way out.
questions.lesson_line: Read the chain before you trade: the bid, the ask, the volume and the open interest.

wrong.The level 2 screen: Level 2 shows the waiting orders on one ticker. The chain lists the contracts.
wrong.Time and sales: Time and sales lists trades as they print. The chain lists the contracts you can pick from.
wrong.The order ticket: The ticket is where you send the order, after you pick from the chain.

questions.simple: The option chain, the table of every contract on a stock by expiry and strike.

questions.story: Your Journal labels a trade Call Credit Spread: sell the 60 call, buy the 65 call, same expiry.
questions.q: Where does this trade do best?
questions.why: Below $60. A call credit spread is a bear call spread. If the stock stays under your short 60 strike, both calls expire worthless and you keep the whole credit. The worst case is the stock above $65. Then you lose the gap between the strikes, less the credit you took in.
questions.lesson_line: A call credit spread wants the stock under the short strike.

wrong.Stock rallies above $65: Above $65 is the worst case: the gap between the strikes, less the credit.
wrong.Stock sits right at $65: At $65 the short call is in the money by the full gap. That's already the max loss.
wrong.Stock moves far either way: That's what a long straddle wants. This trade wants the stock to stay down.

questions.simple: Below $60, because then both calls expire worthless and you keep the whole credit.

reasons: rests on the Journal's label (prettyStrategyType), which can change

questions.q: Iron condor for a $1.50 credit. Sell the 65 call, buy the 70 call, sell the 55 put, buy the 50 put. What's your max loss per contract?
questions.why: $350. The stock can only blow through one side, so only one wing can lose. The call wing is 70 minus 65, or 5 wide. Take off the 1.50 credit and you're at 3.50. Times 100 shares is $350. The put side is the same width, so it's $350 either way. Know that number before you sell premium.
questions.lesson_line: Know the max loss before you sell premium. On a condor it's the wing width minus the credit.
questions.simple: $350, because only one side can lose: the 5-wide wing less the $1.50 credit, times 100.

deeper.trap: Don't add both wings together. At expiration the stock is above the top call strike or below the bottom put strike, never both. So only one side's width counts, less the credit you collected.

wrong.$650: You added the credit to the width. Subtract it.
wrong.$1,000: You added both wings. Only one side can lose.
wrong.$500: That's the full width. You forgot the $1.50 credit.

questions.story: You sell a call on a stock you don't own. You have no other position in it.
questions.q: How big can your loss get?
choices: It grows with no cap as the stock rises
It grows with no cap as the stock falls
It stops at the premium you took in
It stops at the strike minus premium
questions.answer: It grows with no cap as the stock rises
questions.why: There's no cap. A naked call loses more the higher the stock goes, and a stock can keep going up. If you're assigned, you have to deliver shares you don't own. The premium is the most you can make, not the most you can lose. That's the opposite of how we use options. For us they're a defined-risk way in, never an open-ended one.
questions.lesson_line: A naked call caps your gain and leaves your loss open.

wrong.It grows with no cap as the stock falls: A short call loses as the stock rises. If it ends below the strike, the call expires worthless and you keep the premium.
wrong.It stops at the premium you took in: The premium is the most you can make, not the most you can lose.
wrong.It stops at the strike minus premium: Nothing caps it. The stock can keep rising, and so does your loss.

questions.simple: There's no cap on the loss, because the stock can keep rising and you'd have to deliver shares.

deeper.trap: Don't read the premium as the risk. The premium is the most a naked call writer can make. The worst case is a stock that keeps rising, so the loss has no ceiling.

questions.q: Write a naked put, and the most you can lose is the premium you collected.
questions.why: False. The premium is the most you can make. The worst case is the stock going to zero. Then you still have to buy it at the strike, so you lose the strike less the premium. A put writer's risk is smaller than a naked call's, but it's still big. Selling a put means agreeing to buy the stock, so plan on owning it.
questions.lesson_line: Selling a put means agreeing to buy the stock. Plan on owning it.
questions.simple: False, because if the stock goes to zero you still must buy it at the strike.

deeper.trap: Don't call a put writer's risk small just because it has a floor. The floor is zero. If the stock collapses, you still buy at the strike.

questions.story: You sold a covered call on 100 shares. The stock ran through the strike. This morning your shares are gone and cash at the strike sits in their place.
questions.q: What happened to you?
questions.why: You were assigned. A holder exercised, and the notice landed on you, the writer. OCC hands those out at random. On a short call you deliver the shares and get the strike price in cash. That's the deal you made when you sold the call. If you want to keep the shares, buy the call back before it gets that far.
questions.lesson_line: When a holder exercises, a writer gets assigned. On a call, you hand over the shares.

wrong.Exercise: Exercise was the holder's move. What happened to you, the writer, is assignment.
wrong.Expiration: Expiration is just the end date. Your shares went because a holder exercised.
wrong.Rolling: Rolling is your own trade: close the call and open another. Your shares would still be there.

questions.simple: You were assigned, because a holder exercised and you, the writer, had to deliver the shares.

deeper.trap: You don't get a say in who's assigned. OCC assigns exercises at random to clearing members, and your broker passes the notice to a customer short that series.

questions.q: You're short a call on a US stock. You can be assigned on any trading day before it expires, not just at expiration.
questions.why: True. US stock options are American-style, so the holder can exercise any day. That means you can be assigned any day the market's open. The odds go up as the option gets deeper in the money and as expiration gets close. To be safe on a given day, close the short before that day's close.
questions.lesson_line: Short an option and you're on call every trading day.
questions.simple: True, because the holder can exercise any trading day, so you can be assigned any trading day.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking assignment waits for expiration day. With an American-style option it can come on any trading day. It gets more likely deep in the money and near expiry. Only closing the short before that day's close takes the risk away for that day.

questions.q: You own a European-style index option. You're stuck in it until expiration day.
questions.why: False. European style limits when you can exercise, not when you can trade. You can sell it back in the market any day before expiration. Most index options are European-style, so you'll run into this. Exercise style and getting out are two different things.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise style limits exercising, not trading. You can always sell it in the market.
questions.simple: False, because European style only limits exercise, and you can still sell the option any day.

deeper.trap: Do not mix up exercise and trading. Most index options are European-style, so you cannot exercise them early. You can still sell them back in the market any day before expiration. Exercise style limits only exercise.

reasons: European exercise window is worded differently across OIC and FINRA pages (in conflicts)

questions.story: Your call expires today and closes $0.03 in the money. You never told your broker what to do with it.
questions.q: Under OCC's standard rules, what happens?
questions.why: It gets exercised for you. At expiration, OCC exercises equity options a penny or more in the money, unless you tell your broker not to. Your broker may also use its own cutoff. So you could wake up owning the shares and owing the money for them. Don't leave it to chance. Sell it or give clear instructions before the close.
questions.lesson_line: Never leave an expiring option to chance. Close it or tell your broker.

wrong.It expires worthless: That's what happens to an option out of the money. Yours is in the money.
wrong.It's sold at the close: A sale takes an order from you. A penny in the money means exercise.
wrong.It rolls to next month: Rolling is a trade you choose. Nothing rolls on its own.

questions.simple: It's exercised for you, because OCC exercises expiring options a penny or more in the money unless you say no.

deeper.trap: Exercise by exception is OCC's standard procedure, and your broker may use a different threshold. If the call is exercised, you buy the stock at the strike and end up holding shares. OIC's advice: give your broker explicit instructions to exercise, or not, on any expiring option.

reasons: OCC's $.01 threshold and broker thresholds can change

questions.story: You're short the 50 call. At Friday's expiration close, the stock sits at exactly $50.00.
questions.q: What risk are you carrying into the weekend?
questions.why: Pin risk. With the stock sitting right on your strike, you don't know if you'll be assigned. A late move or a holder's choice decides it. You could open Monday short the stock, a position you never planned. There's no time value left to decay, so theta isn't the issue. The fix is simple: buy the call back before the close.
questions.lesson_line: When in doubt, close them out.

wrong.Time decay: There's no time value left to decay at expiration.
wrong.Liquidity risk: The market's closed. What's open is whether you get assigned.
wrong.Interest rate risk: That's rho, a pricing input. It doesn't decide whether you're assigned.

questions.simple: Pin risk, because with the stock right at your strike you can't know if you'll be assigned.

deeper.trap: The trap is assuming an option that ends exactly at the money just expires quietly. The writer can't know whether it will be assigned, or whether a last-second move changed things. A short call can turn into a short stock position you never planned. Some investors put it this way: when in doubt, close them out.

questions.q: Open interest in a stock's calls keeps rising. That tells you traders are bullish on it.
questions.why: False. Every open call has a buyer and a seller. The buyer may be bullish, and the seller may be bearish. Open interest counts the contracts, not who's right. On our Options Flow page, look at the print itself: the side, the size and the premium. That tells you more than open interest alone.
questions.lesson_line: Open interest counts positions, not opinions.
questions.simple: False, because every open contract has a buyer and a seller, so rising open interest isn't a vote.

deeper.counter: Open interest rises when a buyer and a writer both open. So every added call has a seller as well as a buyer. Rising call open interest grows from sellers as much as from buyers.

questions.story: A call series shows open interest (OI) of 1,200. Today's only trade: one trader buys 300 to open. The seller was closing 300 calls she owned.
questions.q: What happened to volume and open interest?
questions.why: Volume 300, and open interest stays 1,200. Volume is just what traded today, the 300. Open interest only changes when contracts open or close. The buyer opened 300 and the seller closed 300, so it's 1,200 plus 300 minus 300. That's still 1,200. It only rises when both sides open.
questions.lesson_line: Volume is today's trading. Open interest only grows when both sides open.

wrong.Volume 300, OI up to 1,500: Open interest rises only when both sides open. The seller was closing.
wrong.Volume 600, OI up to 1,500: Volume counts contracts traded, and 300 changed hands. Open interest didn't rise either.
wrong.No volume, OI down to 900: There was a trade, so there's volume. Open interest falls only when both sides close.

questions.simple: Volume is 300 and open interest stays 1,200, because one side opened while the other closed.

deeper.trap: Big volume doesn't mean new positions. If every buyer opens while every seller closes, contracts change hands and open interest stays flat. Our Options Flow page says it on a standard print: check the next day's open interest to confirm.

questions.story: A friend buys calls the day before earnings. The report's good and the stock opens up 2%. Her calls open below what she paid.
questions.q: What most likely hurt her calls?
choices: Delta flipped negative on the gap
questions.why: Implied volatility came down. Into earnings it can get bid up, and after the report it often drops hard. That drop pulls a call's price down even when the stock rises, and here it outweighed the 2% gain. Buy calls the day before a report and you're paying up for the event. You can be right on direction and still lose.
questions.lesson_line: Into earnings you pay up for implied volatility. After the report it often drops.

wrong.Delta flipped negative on the gap: A call's delta runs from 0.00 to 1.00. It can't go negative.
wrong.Open interest dropped overnight: Open interest doesn't set the price. It counts open contracts.
wrong.Her calls were assigned overnight: Only writers get assigned. She owns the calls.

questions.simple: Implied volatility fell after the report, and that pulled her calls down even though the stock rose.

deeper.trap: A good report doesn't mean a call profit. Implied volatility can be bid up ahead of the news and drop sharply after, more so when the report lands softer than expected. That drop can leave a call down with the stock up.

reasons: the story showed a buy the day before earnings, which the owner's rule B22 forbids; reframed onto a friend so the member never models it

questions.story: Before earnings, your platform shows an expected move of $8 on a $100 stock.
questions.q: What does that $8 tell you?
choices: The size of move priced in, either way
The stock is expected to rise $8
Your max loss if you hold the stock
questions.answer: The size of move priced in, either way
questions.why: The size of move priced in, either way. It's an estimate of magnitude from option prices, with no direction and no guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: Use the expected move to size your risk into earnings, not to pick a side.

wrong.It will close between $92 and $108: It's not a promise. The stock can move more or less than what's priced in.
wrong.The stock is expected to rise $8: An expected move has no direction. It covers a move up or down.
wrong.Your max loss if you hold the stock: The stock can move past it. The expected move doesn't cap your loss on shares.

questions.q: You hear traders talk about 0DTE options. They're special contracts the exchange lists the morning they expire.
questions.why: False. 0DTE just means zero days to expiration. It's a normal listed option on its last day, and very few are listed that morning. Every option becomes 0DTE on its final day. What changes is the clock. Time decay tends to speed up near the end, and gamma runs high, so these swing hard either way.
questions.lesson_line: Every option is 0DTE on its last day. The clock runs fastest at the end.
questions.simple: False, because 0DTE just means an option has reached its last day.

deeper.trap: Don't treat 0DTE as its own product with its own rules. It's the same listed option on its final day. What changes is how fast time decay works against you.

reasons: listing practice can change (OIC primer dated June 2023)

questions.story: You're scanning calls for a cheap swing trade. The 0.10-delta call costs $0.15 and looks like a bargain.
questions.q: Read as rough odds, what does that delta say?
choices: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
About a 10% chance it ends worthless
About 15% chance it ends in the money
About 0.1% chance it ends in the money
questions.answer: About a 10% chance it ends in the money
questions.why: About a 10% chance it ends in the money. Some traders read delta as rough odds of finishing in the money. A 0.10 delta needs a strong move just to be worth anything at expiration. So most of the time that $0.15 goes to zero. It's cheap because it probably won't pay. Price the odds, not the ticket.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap options are cheap for a reason. Price the odds, not the ticket.

wrong.About a 10% chance it ends worthless: That flips it. Read as odds, 0.10 is about a 10% chance of ending in the money. Worthless is the likely result.
wrong.About 15% chance it ends in the money: That reads the $0.15 price as the odds. The price is the premium. The 0.10 delta gives about 10%.
wrong.About 0.1% chance it ends in the money: A 0.10 delta read as odds is about 10%, not 0.1%.

questions.simple: About a 10% chance, because some traders read a 0.10 delta as rough odds of ending in the money.

deeper.trap: A $0.15 premium looks small. Read as odds, though, a 0.10 delta call mostly finishes out of the money, and then the whole premium is gone. The low price reflects low odds, not a bargain.

reasons: delta as probability is a trader convention, not a definition (in conflicts)

questions.story: You own 100 shares of a leader you think can run for months. A friend tells you to sell covered calls on it for income.
questions.q: What's the catch?
choices: Your upside is capped at the strike
You lose the premium if it falls
questions.answer: Your upside is capped at the strike
questions.why: Your upside gets capped at the strike. While the call is open, you give up most of the run past it. Rally through the strike and your shares likely get called away, right in the middle of the move you were holding for. The premium is yours either way. That's small money next to a big winner. On a leader, I don't want a lid on the run.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sell calls on a leader you're holding for the big move.

wrong.Your downside risk becomes unlimited: The short call adds no downside. The shares carry the same risk they did.
wrong.You must buy 100 more shares: Your 100 shares already cover one call. There's nothing more to buy.
wrong.You lose the premium if it falls: You keep the premium whatever the stock does. The buyer paid it to you.

questions.simple: Your upside is capped at the strike, which hurts most on a stock you expect to run.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word income. You keep the premium whatever happens, but while the call is open you give up much of the upside. If the stock rallies past the strike, the shares are likely to be called away, in the middle of the run you held for.

questions.q: You buy one call for $2.00. If the stock tanks, you can lose more than the $2.00 a share you paid.
questions.why: False. Buying an option, the most you can lose is what you paid. If the stock is under the strike at expiration, the whole $2.00 is gone, and that's it. The open-ended loss sits with the writer. Capped doesn't mean small, though. Size it like all of it can go, because it can.
questions.lesson_line: Your loss on a bought option stops at the premium. Plan on losing all of it.
questions.simple: False, because a call buyer can only lose the premium paid, and no more.

deeper.trap: Don't confuse a capped loss with a small one. All of the premium can go if the call ends below the strike at expiration. Size the trade as if the whole premium will be lost.

questions.q: You buy a standard monthly call on a stock. Unless a holiday moves it, its last trading day is the third Friday of the month.
questions.why: True. Standard monthly stock options stop trading on the third Friday of the expiration month. If that Friday's an exchange holiday, the last day is the Thursday before. Lots of stocks also list weekly options, so don't assume. Read the exact date on the contract before you buy it.
questions.lesson_line: Read the date on every contract. Not every option ends on the third Friday.
questions.simple: True, because standard monthly stock options stop trading on the third Friday, or the Thursday before a holiday.

deeper.trap: Not every option ends on the third Friday. Many stocks list weekly expirations, and a holiday moves the last trading day to the Thursday before. Read the exact date on each contract you trade.

reasons: expiration schedule is a date rule that can change

questions.story: A setup triggers, and you buy one call instead of the shares. The call is quoted at $2.00.
questions.q: Where's your stop on the call?
choices: Sell if the call loses half
Just under the stock's day low
questions.why: The full premium you paid. On an option, the premium paid is the stop. That's $2.00 a share here, and you plan on losing all of it. We trade shares, and we use options only now and then, as a defined-risk way in. So size the call so losing the whole $2.00 is a loss you're fine with. Don't bolt a share-style stop onto it.
questions.simple: The full premium, because on an option the premium paid is the stop.
questions.lesson_line: On an option, the premium paid is the stop. Size it so losing all of it is fine.

wrong.Sell if the call loses half: We don't add a cut like that. The premium paid is the stop.
wrong.Just under the stock's day low: That's how we stop out shares, a few cents under the day's low. On an option, the premium is the stop.
wrong.About 3% under your entry: On shares the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. On an option, the premium is the stop.

reasons: house rule (sizing_rule.md section 9, A6 and B25)

conflicts: Expiration day: the SEC's options bulletin (updated July 16, 2026) still says the expiration date is 'generally the Saturday after the third Friday'. OIC's current glossary (Expiration Friday) and Options Basics say standard equity options generally have their last trading day, and usually expire, on the third Friday. q66 follows OIC and is phrased as the last trading day; no question uses the SEC's Saturday line.

European-style wording differs: OIC's glossary and FINRA say 'only during a specified period just prior to expiration'; OIC's FAQ: Basics says 'only on its expiration date'; OIC's FAQ: Options Exercise says the last trading day. q20 and q55 say 'only at expiration' / 'at or just before expiration', which all three support, and q55 keys on OIC's line that a European-style position can still be closed in the market any day.

Exercise statistics disagree across OIC's own FAQs ('more than 72%' closed before expiration, 'about 70%' sold to close, 'about 7%' exercised; FINRA also says about 7%). No question keys any percentage; q19's lesson avoids 'most holders sell'.

Exercise by exception: OCC's threshold is $.01 in the money (OIC FAQs), but OIC says 'your firm may have a different threshold', and some brokers act on expiring positions under their own risk rules. q56 asks only what happens 'under OCC's standard procedure' and its why and lesson tell the member to give the broker instructions.

Delta as probability is a trader's convention, not a definition: OIC says 'Some traders view Delta as a percentage probability'. q63 asks it as 'read as a rough probability'; q21 lists it as how some traders read delta.

Expected move: no single official definition. OIC (Rule of 16 takeaways) says an implied-volatility move 'describes magnitude of expected movement, not direction'; Schwab's Market Maker Move page says the figure guarantees no size and no direction. q61 keys only on those shared points and uses the generic phrase 'expected move', not a platform's indicator name.

Iron condor naming: OIC files the credit iron condor as 'Short Condor (Iron Condor)' and calls the iron butterfly the 'Short Iron Butterfly'. Questions use the common names (iron condor, iron butterfly) for the credit versions, matching the Journal's labels, and cite the OIC pages for the structure and the max loss.

Journal labels vs textbook names: the Journal's 'Put Credit Spread' and 'Call Credit Spread' are OIC's bull put spread and bear call spread (OIC's own page titles carry both names, and its glossary lists both as credit spreads). q36 and q49 teach that mapping.

Seen and NOT used: OIC's glossary entry on strike price intervals gives old standard increments while saying many stocks are exempt; OIC's FAQ gives an exercise cut-off of 4:30 p.m. CT for exchanges (time-sensitive, broker cut-offs are earlier); FINRA's assignment page says SPX options are 'tied to S&P 500 futures contracts' (SPX options are on the index); OIC's open interest article has a typo in its third example (Trader A's position 'transferred to Trader B' where it means C). No fact or question relies on these; q59 uses only the article's summary rules.

Investopedia's options-chain page says higher volume and open interest mean options 'are more easily traded and have tighter bid-ask spreads'; OIC's FAQ calls equating volume and open interest with liquidity 'a common misconception' and points to the quoted market and its size. q17 and q58 stay on what open interest counts; q48 cites the Investopedia page only for what a chain lists.
Taxes: OIC's General Information FAQ mentions the wash-sale rule. Out of scope by the owner's ruling (ask a tax professional); nothing here touches it.
